analysis.one_liner: Lifts protections from roadless national forest lands and BLM wilderness study areas, opening them to road building and development.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 47 cosponsors and a July 2011 subcommittee hearing, then died in committee without ever getting a House vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have released Bureau of Land Management wilderness study areas that the agency had identified as not suitable for wilderness, and inventoried roadless areas in national forests that were not recommended for wilderness, from continued management to preserve their roadless and wilderness character [S2][S3]. Those lands would have been managed under standard land-use plans that allow road construction, logging, and other development [S3]. It also would have barred the Interior and Agriculture Secretaries from issuing system-wide rules to re-protect the released lands, and ended the applicability of the 2010 BLM Wildlands Order on them [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Timber companies would gain access to build roads and log in inventoried roadless national forest areas; mining and oil and gas companies would gain access to areas currently managed to stay undeveloped; and off-road vehicle users would gain motorized access. Some local governments in resource-dependent counties argued the release would expand economic activity.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Timber, mining, and oil and gas companies

how_it_helps.text: Declares that BLM lands identified as unsuitable for wilderness have been adequately studied and are no longer subject to the requirement that wilderness study areas be managed so wilderness remains an option, returning them to the applicable land-use plan.

Releases inventoried roadless areas in the National Forest System that were not recommended for wilderness from the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule and the 2005 State Petitions rule, so they are no longer managed to maintain roadless character.

Prohibits the Interior and Agriculture Secretaries from issuing any system-wide regulation, directive, or order that would manage the released lands contrary to the applicable land-use plan, preventing an agency from re-imposing protection across the board.
Ends the applicability of BLM Wildlands Order 3310 on the released lands.

analysis.who_pays: Americans who hunt, fish, hike, and rely on public lands for intact backcountry would lose the roadless and wilderness protections on these areas; downstream communities that depend on forested watersheds for clean water would bear the effects of road building and development; and the public would lose options that currently remain open for future wilderness designation.

drawbacks.text: The bill would end management to maintain the roadless character of inventoried national forest areas, removing the restrictions of the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule that keep them undeveloped.

It would lift BLM's obligation to manage wilderness study areas so that their suitability for preservation as wilderness is not impaired, foreclosing wilderness designation on lands the agency found unsuitable even where local land-use plans would allow development.

By barring system-wide protective rules, the bill would prevent federal land agencies from re-imposing roadless or wilderness protections on the released lands by regulation, leaving only future acts of Congress as a check.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Supporters' good-faith argument is that millions of acres were locked into de facto wilderness status by regulation without a congressional decision, limiting logging, grazing, energy access, and even some forest-health work in areas the land agencies themselves had not recommended for wilderness. The counterweight is that roadless protections are what keep backcountry habitat, hunting and fishing grounds, and clean-water watersheds intact, and releasing them through a single act of Congress—with agency-wide protective rules prohibited—would have been hard to undo. The bill never advanced far enough for Congress to weigh those trade-offs on the record.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees, got one subcommittee hearing in July 2011, and then sat without any committee or floor vote until the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Kevin McCarthy of California introduced the bill on April 15, 2011, joined by 22 original cosponsors listed in the bill text.
It attracted 47 total cosponsors, 45 Republicans and 2 Democrats.
The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and the House Agriculture Committee on the day of introduction.

It was referred to the Natural Resources Subcommittee on National Parks, Forests and Public Lands on April 22, 2011, and to the Agriculture Subcommittee on Conservation, Energy, and Forestry on May 11, 2011.
A subcommittee hearing was held on July 26, 2011; that was the last recorded action on the bill.
Neither committee ever reported the bill, and the House never voted on it before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, roadless national forest areas and BLM wilderness study areas kept their existing protections, and timber, mining, and energy companies gained no new access to them. Public-lands users who value intact backcountry came out ahead; the industries that sponsored the bill came out with nothing.

for.name: Rep. Kevin McCarthy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Wilderness and Roadless Area Release Act of 2011 and recruited original cosponsors.

for.name: Timber, mining, and energy interests
for.what_they_did: Backed the release of roadless and wilderness study areas for development access.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to subcommittee, held one hearing on July 26, 2011, and took no further action, never reporting it to the House.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Conservation, Energy, and Forestry and took no further action.

against.name: Conservation and sportsmen's groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill as a threat to roadless forests and wilderness study areas.

sides.party_line_note: Of the bill's 47 cosponsors, 45 were Republicans and 2 were Democrats; the sponsor and all listed original cosponsors were Republicans.

industries.note: Releasing inventoried roadless areas from the 2001 Roadless Rule would allow road construction and logging in national forest areas currently managed to stay undeveloped. The industry's gain comes directly from opening backcountry that hunters, anglers, and recreationists use.

industries.industry: Mining and oil and gas companies
industries.note: Lands released from wilderness-study and roadless management return to standard multiple-use plans under which mineral and energy development is permitted. Removing protections forecloses the public option of designating these areas as wilderness later.

Releasing roadless areas opens them to road building and motorized access that current restrictions do not allow. The gain comes at the cost of the quiet, undeveloped character that other users value.
Guides, outfitters, and tourism economies built on intact backcountry would face opened lands, more roads, and industrial activity in areas now managed as roadless or wilderness study areas.
